title: Superconducting Chip Claims: Don't Change Process Node, Change Temperature Zone — 28nm Logic Can Hit 5nm Performance
dek: Move logic to liquid-helium temperatures and replace transistors with superconducting switches — that's Snowcap's bet: first tape out a RISC-V chip, then claim 28nm-class logic can deliver 5nm-class performance.
why: If you care about the compute power wall, this episode offers a third path — not squeezing transistors, but moving the entire logic to liquid-helium temperatures; a former Intel CEO has placed his bet. The risks and numbers are laid out, worth a listen.
who: Hard-tech investors who want to verify whether superconducting computing is a real path or just a story, and CPU/supercomputer architects studying the chip power wall.
skip: If you're familiar with overclocking and liquid-nitrogen cooling, you can skip the overclocking preamble from 0:00 to 2:01.

points.h: The ceiling for extreme overclocking is heat dissipation, not the chip
points.body: The episode opens with the overclocking industry: everyday chips rely on air cooling, higher-power ones use water cooling, and beyond that you need dry ice, liquid nitrogen, and other sub-zero media. Extreme overclockers push voltage to chase maximum frequencies, making chips hotter, so they need ever more extreme cooling. The host says he was once an extreme overclocker and held the world No. 2 spot — though only for a day and a half. His key reference: such overclocking is only to run a few minutes of benchmarks at 8.5GHz, whereas true superconducting computing isn't about instantaneous records but about logic that runs at near-zero power.

points.h: Liquid-helium overclocking's real cost is the transfer line, not the helium
points.body: Going from liquid nitrogen to liquid helium, physics starts to interfere. Liquid helium costs about 20 times as much as liquid nitrogen (which is about a dollar per liter), but that's not the main expense: the transfer line that moves liquid helium from a large storage tank into a 3-4 kg copper overclocking pot costs $5,000 per use. Intel and Asus have both done liquid-helium overclocking, with records already past 9GHz. The host warns that material behavior changes drastically at such temperatures — some platforms have a 'cold bug' where the system simply won't start when too cold; only platforms without the cold bug are suitable for liquid-helium play.

points.h: Superconductivity's lure isn't speed — it's zero resistance
points.body: Overclocking squeezes frequency out of existing materials; superconductivity is another narrative: electrons flow through superconducting materials with no resistance, making transport effectively free. Currently, most superconductors require extremely low temperatures, and room-temperature superconductivity remains in a state of repeated research claims. The key extrapolation here: if the entire chip's switching logic could operate in a superconducting state, per-operation energy would be 'orders of magnitude' better than current laptops. The host deliberately makes a strong claim but pulls back — superconductivity is still a holy grail, not yet in hand. This sets the stage for Snowcap's entry.

points.h: The former Intel CEO is betting on temperature zone, not process node
points.body: Snowcap Compute just completed a seed round, and its board includes former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger. Their bet is on building superconducting chips that run at about 4-15K, the liquid-helium temperature range. Structurally, it's no longer billions of transistors but a new type of switch that works at superconducting temperatures — the Josephson junction. For now, Snowcap's goal is to first produce a RISC-V-class CPU at low temperature, making power consumption nearly free; the cost is that the entire machine must stay in the liquid-helium temperature range, and cooling itself consumes energy.

points.h: The new variable for superconducting logic is fitting into standard EDA flows
points.body: Long-term researchers are not scarce: U.S. defense contractors have built chips integrating tens of millions of Josephson junctions, and IMEC has reached hundreds of millions, along with supporting logic and EDA tools. Snowcap's differentiator is compatibility: they say this superconducting logic can fit into standard EDA flows and can be taped out on ordinary CMOS processes, using niobium titanium nitride as the material. The core conclusion the host heard: superconductivity's energy-efficiency advantage is equivalent to using 28nm logic to achieve performance close to a 5nm chip — note this isn't a smaller process node but an equivalent gain from lower power.

points.h: Cryo CMOS is only a waypoint; the real hurdle is scale
points.body: Snowcap plans to deliver its first chip in 2026, followed by a deployable RISC-V design. The waypoint can be seen in cryo CMOS: it runs in the liquid-nitrogen range of about 72-77K, and while not superconducting, the low temperature itself lowers power. The real hurdle is crossing from cryo CMOS into superconductivity; the host's skepticism is 'can you scale up performance at high levels' — running and large-scale commercialization are two different things.

points.h: Cold startup isn't rare; the hard part is keeping the whole machine in liquid helium
points.body: This section provides a real-world footnote on cold tape-outs: AMD's first Zen 1 A0 sample, leaked when the company was most cash-strapped, could only start at sub-zero temperatures on dry ice due to a design flaw, later fixed to run at room temperature. So low temperatures in testing and startup aren't unusual; but keeping an entire processor in the liquid-helium range involves infrastructure issues, including helium supply — liquid helium is also the lifeblood of MRI superconducting magnets, and there was a helium shortage a few years back.

points.h: Snowcap isn't selling IP — it's selling a sealed appliance
points.body: Snowcap positions itself not as an IP seller but as delivering complete systems. The host's judgment: precisely because of the infrastructure barrier of the liquid-helium range, the product will be nearly a sealed appliance, and the software stack will need to be rebuilt. A seed-stage company still has Series A/B/C rounds to get through; but they've already brought in advisors and former employees from Apple, Nvidia, and Google. On this topic, skepticism is warranted, but so is follow-up.
